manifest.name: dsh-ai-model-hub
manifest.description: DeepSeek Harness plugin and library for local AI models: a capability catalog, router, runtime manager, and real engine adapters. The agent names a capability; the hub selects, starts, and calls a suitable model.

bundle.text:
# dsh-ai-model-hub — DeepSeek Harness plugin bundle patch
#
# This is the `dsh.bundle.patch` layer of the package. When the plugin is
# installed through the official CLI —
#
#   dsh plugin --profile <name> add dsh-ai-model-hub
#   dsh plugin --profile <name> add github:Mhmd7-7/dsh-ai-model-hub
#   dsh plugin --profile <name> add /absolute/path/to/dsh-ai-model-hub
#
# — the command reconciles `dsh.profile.bundles` against installed packages and,
# seeing this declaration, appends the package to the bundle stack. Profile boot
# then merges THIS patch (a single `insert` of the plugin row), so no profile
# file needs editing by hand and the plugin is live on every boot.
#
# NOTE on the two names, which are easy to conflate and fail loudly if you do:
#   `id`   is this row's own name in the composed tree — what a profile's own
#          cordis.patch.yml uses to override or disable the row.
#   `name` is the Node module specifier the loader imports. It MUST be the bare
#          package name: the package's "." export is the plugin
#          (`lib/dsh-plugin/index.js`, exporting `name`/`inject`/`apply`).
#          It must NOT be a subpath (`dsh-ai-model-hub/plugin`): DSH's client
#          module system resolves a row's package manifest only from a bare
#          specifier, so a subpath would silently drop the Web UI half.
#
# Configuration is optional. Every field has a default that makes the
# zero-config case work: the catalog is discovered from ordered anchors (an
# explicit configPath, then `searchRoots`, then the host process's working
# directory, then this package's own installation directory), artifacts land in
# the calling session's workspace, and — importantly — process launching is
# DISABLED, so the hub will talk to engines you run but will never start one.
#
# To configure, uncomment and adjust. See docs/security.md before enabling
# `allowProcessLaunch`, and docs/adding-a-model.md for the catalog format.
#
- insert:
    - id: dsh-ai-model-hub
      name: 'dsh-ai-model-hub'
      # config:
      #   # Explicit catalog path. When set it is the ONLY candidate tried, so a
      #   # wrong path is an error rather than a silent fallback. Omitted =>
      #   # discovery from ordered anchors: `searchRoots`, then the host process's
      #   # working directory, then this package's own installation directory. At
      #   # each level: models.json, model-catalog.json, or dsh-ai-model-hub.json,
      #   # directly or in a config/ subdirectory.
      #   configPath: ''
      #
      #   # Extra directories to start discovery from, in priority order. Use this
      #   # to point the hub at the workspace you actually serve without pinning
      #   # an exact file.
      #   searchRoots: []
      #
      #   # Where produced artifacts are stored. Omitted (the normal case) => each
      #   # tool call writes under the CALLING SESSION's workspace, at
      #   # <workspace>/artifacts, resolved per call from DSH's sandbox policy. Set it
      #   # to one absolute directory only to collect every session's output centrally.
      #   artifactRoot: ''
      #
      #   # Let the hub start and stop model processes. Requires the model's own
      #   # descriptor to declare `lifecycle.startable: true` with a `start` command;
      #   # both must agree before anything launches.
      #   allowProcessLaunch: false
      #
      #   # Permit launch commands outside the built-in engine allowlist
      #   # (python, ollama, llama-server, comfy, blender, ...). Refused engines
      #   # include sh, bash, cmd, powershell, curl, wget, nc.
      #   allowAnyCommand: false
      #
      #   # Give the agent a dynamic snapshot of which capabilities this machine can
      #   # serve, generated from the live catalog so it cannot drift.
      #   exposeCapabilityContext: true
      #
      #   # How to react to a missing or invalid catalog. 'warn' logs the problem,
      #   # registers no tools, and still lets DeepSeek Harness boot; 'throw' fails
      #   # the plugin load, which is what you want while editing a catalog.
      #   onConfigError: warn
      #
      #   # Background probe cadence, in milliseconds. 0 disables each loop.
      #   healthIntervalMs: 30000
      #   idleSweepIntervalMs: 15000
      #
      #   # Default cooperative budget for one invoke_model call.
      #   invocationTimeoutMs: 600000
      #
      #   # Runtime model discovery. OFF by default: the catalog is then exactly the
      #   # document on disk. Set true and the hub also asks every configured host
      #   # what it currently has — a pulled Ollama model, a checkpoint dropped into
      #   # ComfyUI's models directory — and adds those to the catalog with no JSON
      #   # edit. Static entries always win an id collision, and an engine that is
      #   # down is a warning rather than a failed boot.
      #   discoverModels: false
      #
      #   # How long a discovery pass stays cached. The refresh_model_discovery tool
      #   # bypasses it, which is the path for "I just pulled a new model".
      #   discoveryTtlMs: 60000
      #
      #   # Budget for one engine's discovery pass. Raise it if ComfyUI's
      #   # /object_info is slow on your machine.
      #   discoveryTimeoutMs: 5000
      #
      #   # A directory of ComfyUI workflow JSON files for the Local models scan.
      #   # The scan already reads the workflows ComfyUI has saved — through the
      #   # engine's own /userdata route while it answers, and from its own
      #   # saved-workflow store on disk while it does not — and this is the
      #   # additional source for workflows kept beside the catalog. Every *.json
      #   # file under it is read, recursively. A relative path is resolved against
      #   # the catalog, and %VAR% and ~/ are expanded.
      #   #
      #   # It is a source of WORKFLOWS only. Nothing here (or anywhere else on
      #   # that page) enumerates checkpoints, LoRAs, VAEs or custom nodes: those
      #   # belong to the workflow that uses them.
      #   comfyuiWorkflowDir: ''
      #
      #   # Budget for each probe, in milliseconds; directory walks also have
      #   # count/depth/deadline limits. Opening or reloading the page only LOOKS;
      #   # pressing Scan starts the configured engines, waits for their APIs, and
      #   # releases them when it finishes. Scan never stops an engine that was
      #   # already running, and never installs anything.
      #   scanTimeoutMs: 4000
      #
      #   # How long one engine may take to answer after Scan starts it, in
      #   # milliseconds. 0 (the default) means "use the host's own declared
      #   # startupTimeoutMs, then a per-engine default" — ComfyUI gets 300s,
      #   # because loading checkpoints takes minutes; Ollama gets 120s. Set it to
      #   # put a shorter leash on a cold start.
      #   engineStartupTimeoutMs: 0
      #
      #   # Where the workflows a scan discovers are remembered, so they stay
      #   # listed while ComfyUI is stopped — including on a first launch, where
      #   # the local files are the only source there is. Omitted =>
      #   # ~/.dsh/plugins/dsh-ai-model-hub/workflow-catalog.json.
      #   workflowCatalogPath: ''
      #
      #   # Where the saved capability policy lives. The policy — the per-capability
      #   # order and enable/disable decisions made on the Local models page — is
      #   # YOUR data, so it is stored in its own versioned document rather than
      #   # being derived from the catalog or written into the profile's generated
      #   # configuration. Omitted => ~/.dsh/plugins/dsh-ai-model-hub/
      #   # capability-policy.json.
      #   policyPath: ''
      #
      #   # The most capability options ONE request may attempt. Omitted (the
      #   # shipping default) walks the WHOLE permitted list, so a saved order of
      #   # ten options really is ten attempts. Set it only if you want a smaller
      #   # budget, and note that the failure message then reports how many options
      #   # went untried instead of implying they failed.
      #   attemptBudget: 0
      #
      #   # Offer the subscription plugin's image, video and conversational backends
      #   # as capability options. Harmless when that plugin is absent: a profile
      #   # without it registers nothing and logs one line. Every subscription
      #   # option is DISABLED until you enable it, which is what keeps discovery,
      #   # catalog presence and a descriptor's own flags from authorizing spend on
      #   # your subscription.
      #   integrateSubscriptions: true

readme.section: dsh-ai-model-hub
readme.text:
A modular local AI model ecosystem for **DeepSeek Harness (DSH)**.

DSH is the agent — it reasons, plans, calls tools, and orchestrates workflows.
It is **not** the model runtime. The specialised models (text, image, 3D, audio,
video) are external and local, reached through a capability interface. DSH never
learns how to launch Stable Diffusion, which Python file starts a mesh generator,
or how a given engine manages its process. It only asks:

> **What capabilities are available?**

readme.section: dsh-ai-model-hub
readme.text:
Everything below that question is this project's job.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  DeepSeek Harness                        agent reasoning, planning,  │
│  ─────────────────                       tool invocation, workflows  │
│                                                                      │

---

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
**Live as a DSH profile plugin.** The package installs as one unit — `dsh plugin
add` mounts it, so the hub is composed on every boot — and it serves **real local
engines only**: Ollama for text, ComfyUI / A1111 / Forge for images, llama.cpp for
a second text engine, and any local image-to-3D Gradio app for meshes. There are no
mock models anywhere in the shipped catalogs and no mock fallback at runtime: a
wrong model name or a stopped engine is a loud error (or a cold start), never
fixture output.

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
The whole architecture — catalog → routing → runtime → adapter → artifact →
chained workflow — is covered by the test suite, which uses an in-process **mock
adapter as a test double**. That adapter is not a model: nothing ships it in a
catalog, and no deployment can reach it by accident.

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
| Phase | Scope | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Full architecture, DSH plugin, tests | ✅ done |
| 2 | Real local text model (Ollama / llama.cpp / vLLM / LM Studio) | ✅ done — `openai_compatible` adapter ships |
| 3 | Real local image model (A1111 / ComfyUI) | ✅ done — `http_json` and `comfyui` adapters ship |
| 4 | Real local 3D model | ✅ done — `three_d` adapter ships; see [docs/three-d.md](docs/three-d.md) |
| 5 | Runtime lifecycle + resource-aware routing | ✅ done — the machine is probed and routed against |
| 6 | Multi-model workflows | ✅ done |

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
Phase 2 needs no new code: the `openai_compatible` adapter is implemented, and
`config/examples/real-models.example.json` contains ready-to-copy Ollama and
llama.cpp entries. Phase 3 is implemented by **two** adapters, because the two
engine families are genuinely different:

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
- **`http_json`** — engines that answer one request with a finished image:
  AUTOMATIC1111, Forge, and `stable-diffusion.cpp`'s `sd-server`. It POSTs the
  familiar `/sdapi/v1/txt2img` body and decodes the base64 images that come back.
- **`comfyui`** — ComfyUI takes an API-format *node graph*, not a prompt endpoint.
  Each explicitly configured workflow declares capabilities, exact input bindings
  and a typed output selector. The adapter treats graph internals as opaque, edits
  only declared inputs, queues on `/prompt`, polls `/history`, and retrieves the
  declared output. No checkpoint or saved-workflow enumeration creates providers.

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
Phase 4 is **`three_d`**: one adapter that speaks the shape the local 3D ecosystem
actually has — a Gradio queue API or a JSON HTTP route, one or two calls, a mesh
file at the end — so TRELLIS, Hunyuan3D, Stable Fast 3D, and TripoSR are catalog
entries rather than code. It writes a typed `model_3d` artifact (GLB, GLTF, OBJ,
STL, or PLY, sniffed from the bytes), and a discoverer verifies a declared engine
against the API surface it actually exposes before publishing anything.

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
Phase 5's remaining gap is closed: `ModelHub` now probes RAM, VRAM, free VRAM, and
disk, re-measures on demand, and routes against measured **headroom** — so a model
that would not fit beside what is already loaded is refused with the shortfall in
the message instead of crashing inside the engine.

readme.section: Status
readme.text:
All adapters are registered by default. See
[docs/adding-a-model.md](docs/adding-a-model.md), [docs/three-d.md](docs/three-d.md),
and the protocol templates in [`config/workflows/`](config/workflows/).

---

readme.section: Install
readme.text:
One command, on a machine that already has Node ≥ 22.6 and DeepSeek Harness:

```sh

readme.section: into the profile behind `dsh web` — the normal case
readme.text:
dsh plugin --profile web add github:Mhmd7-7/dsh-ai-model-hub
```

This package **is** the plugin: it declares `dsh.bundle.patch`, so `dsh plugin
add` installs it *and* appends `dsh-ai-model-hub` to `dsh.profile.bundles`. The
profile composes that bundle on every boot, which is what makes the plugin
List the available AI model capabilities.
```

readme.section: into the profile behind `dsh web` — the normal case
readme.text:
| What you want | Command |
|---|---|
| Another profile | `dsh plugin --profile hubtest add github:Mhmd7-7/dsh-ai-model-hub` |powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mhmd7-7/dsh-ai-model-hub/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mhmd7-7/dsh-ai-model-hub/main/install.sh | sh
```

To remove an installation:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web remove dsh-ai-model-hub
```

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
The plugin tracks the DSH `0.x` line rather than a single release:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Supported** | `@deepseek-ai/dsh*` `>=0.1.5-rc.2 <0.3.0` |
| **Developed and tested against** | `0.1.5-rc.2` (this package's own tree) and `0.2.0-rc.2` (a current host) |

Two independent things decide whether that holds, and they fail in different
places — which is worth knowing, because only one of them is visible in the
plugin's own logs.

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
**The manifest gate runs first, before any plugin code.** DSH reads
`peerDependencies` and refuses the row when a `@deepseek-ai/dsh*` range does not
match the harness. For a `0.x` version, **caret pins the minor**: `^0.1.5-rc.2`
means `>=0.1.5-rc.2 <0.2.0`, so it silently refuses every `0.2.x` host. That is
why the peers here are written as explicit ranges and why
`tests/peer-range.test.ts` exists — it asserts against the harness's own
`evaluatePluginCompatibility` when that package is installed, and against a
written-out range matcher when it is not. The old caret form is demonstrated
failing in the same file, so it cannot come back unnoticed.

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
**Then the runtime surface is detected, not assumed.** `dsh-plugin/compat.ts` is
the only module that touches a host member. It reads the context once, reports
what it found, and every registration goes through a helper that contains a
missing or differently-shaped member to one diagnostic line:

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
| If the host has no… | What is lost | What is **not** lost |
|---|---|---|
| `tools` | everything | nothing — the load fails, by name, on purpose |
| `systemPrompt` | the capability snapshot in the prompt | every tool; the agent can still call `list_capabilities` |
| `webServer` | the Local models and Priorities pages | every tool |
| `effect` | stopping the hub's processes on plugin unload | every tool; the effect body is not run at all, because nothing could call its disposer |
| `skills` | the bundled skill | every tool |
| `sandboxPolicy` | artifacts in the calling session's workspace | every tool; artifacts fall back to the hub's own store |
| `get` | nothing | the injected-property path still resolves every optional service |
| `logger` | host-formatted diagnostics | the diagnostics — they go to the console instead |

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
`tools` is the one hard requirement. Without a tool registry there is nothing for
this plugin to do, and a hub the agent cannot reach is worse than an honest
failure: it produces a settings page and the false impression that the capability
is available.

readme.section: Which DeepSeek Harness versions this runs on
readme.text:
Two things are deliberately **not** wrapped. `defineTool`, because it is a pure
function from a closed input to a closed output whose signature has not moved
across the whole `0.1.5-rc` → `0.2.0-rc` line. And the `import type` lines, which
vanish at compile time — a host that renames a type cannot break a running plugin.
The complete runtime DSH coupling is six value imports: `defineTool`,
`schemastery`'s default export, and cordis's `Service`.

readme.section: Why the package ships compiled JavaScript
readme.text:
The plugin's sources are TypeScript, and Node runs them directly through type
stripping while you work in a checkout. It refuses to do that inside
`node_modules`:

```
ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING: Stripping types is currently
unsupported for files under node_modules
```

readme.section: Why the package ships compiled JavaScript
readme.text:
A package installed by name — from GitHub, from a registry — lands *inside* the
profile's `node_modules`, so a `.ts` entry there could never be imported. That is
the entire reason this repository commits `lib/`: `lib/` is the same sources
compiled to JavaScript, and the package's entry points (`main`, `exports`) point
at it, so `dsh plugin add` needs no build step on your machine.

readme.section: Why the package ships compiled JavaScript
readme.text:
`lib/` is generated, never edited: `npm run build` regenerates it from `src/` and
`dsh-plugin/`. The one setting that makes it work is
`rewriteRelativeImportExtensions`, so the emitted JavaScript imports `./x.js`
where the source said `./x.ts`.

---

readme.section: Quick start
readme.text: There are two halves, and you can use either without the other.

readme.section: A. Use the hub as a library (no DSH needed)
readme.text:
```sh
cd dsh-ai-model-hub

npm install                  # typescript + the DSH packages the plugin links against
npm test                     # the suite, ~20 s, no engines or GPU required

The demo prints the full path — capability discovery, routing with reasons,
invocation, and the artifact on disk:

readme.section: A. Use the hub as a library (no DSH needed)
readme.text:
```
=== catalog: capability discovery ===
  text_to_image        text → image  via comfyui_z_image_turbo
  text_to_text         text → text  via ollama_text_model
  not available here: image_to_3d, image_to_image, audio_generation, …

readme.section: A. Use the hub as a library (no DSH needed)
readme.text:
It runs against `config/models.json`, so it needs the engines that catalog names:
Ollama for text, ComfyUI for images. `node examples/vertical-slice.ts <catalog>`
takes another catalog, and the last section deliberately asks for a capability
nobody serves, to show what a refusal looks like.

readme.section: A. Use the hub as a library (no DSH needed)
readme.text:
`npm run demo:3d` needs nothing installed. It starts a stand-in 3D engine inside
the example and runs the *whole* real path against it — discovery, health,
resource-aware routing, a two-step Gradio protocol, and a `.glb` written to disk —
then prints every HTTP request the engine saw, to make the boundary concrete. To
point it at TRELLIS instead, swap the stand-in for your catalog entry; the three
capability calls are identical. See [docs/three-d.md](docs/three-d.md).

readme.section: B. Give the capability to the DeepSeek Harness agent
readme.text: ```sh

readme.section: Installs into the 'web' profile (the one behind `dsh web`), then verifies.
readme.text: npm run install:plugin

readme.section: ...or target another profile:
readme.text:
node --no-deprecation scripts/install-plugin.mjs --profile <name>
```

Then **restart DeepSeek Harness** and ask the agent:

```
List the available AI model capabilities.
```

readme.section: Checking an installation
readme.text:
```sh
npm run doctor                          # inspects: is it loadable, and if not, why not
node scripts/smoke.mjs --profile web    # acts: applies the plugin and lists what it registered
```

`doctor` inspects and reports; `smoke` actually runs the plugin against a real
cordis context and prints the tools it registered. Use `smoke` when you want
proof rather than a checklist:

readme.section: Checking an installation
readme.text:
```
Registered tools:
  check_model_health   explain_routing    get_model_status   invoke_model
  list_artifacts       list_capabilities  list_models        start_model
  stop_model           refresh_model_discovery

> **Note on flags.** `npm run` forwards flags to the script, but npm 12 parses
> `--profile` as its own config flag and fails. Use the direct
> `node scripts/smoke.mjs --profile <name>` form for a non-default profile.

readme.section: If DSH fails to boot after installing
readme.text:
If the harness dies with:

```
invalid plugin, expect function or object with an "apply" method, received object
```

readme.section: If DSH fails to boot after installing
readme.text:
then the row `cordis.patch.yml` inserts is pointing at something that is not a
plugin. In this package that can only happen if the row's `name` was changed
away from the bare package name: `dsh-ai-model-hub` resolves to the package's
`.` export, which is the plugin (`lib/dsh-plugin/index.js`, exporting
`name`/`inject`/`apply`/`Config`). The hub **library** lives behind the
`dsh-ai-model-hub/library` subpath instead, precisely so the two cannot be
confused.

readme.section: If DSH fails to boot after installing
readme.text:
The row has two names, and they are easy to conflate: `id` is the row's name in
the composed tree (what a profile's own `cordis.patch.yml` uses to override or
disable it), while `name` is the module specifier the loader imports. Keep
`name` bare — a subpath such as `dsh-ai-model-hub/plugin` would load the host half
but silently drop the **Web UI half**, because DSH's client module system only
resolves a row's package manifest from a bare specifier. `cordis.patch.yml`
documents this in place, and `npm run doctor` checks it.

readme.section: Where does the catalog come from?
readme.text:
The plugin resolves its catalog from **ordered anchors**, first hit wins:

1. **`configPath`** — an explicit file, if configured. When set it is the only
   candidate: a wrong path is an error, never a silent fallback.
2. Each directory in **`searchRoots`**, for a deployment that names its own.
3. The **working directory of the DSH host process**, walking upward.
4. **This plugin's own installation directory**, walking upward.

readme.section: Where does the catalog come from?
readme.text:
At every level discovery accepts `models.json`, `model-catalog.json`, or
`dsh-ai-model-hub.json`, directly or in a `config/` subdirectory.

readme.section: Where does the catalog come from?
readme.text:
Anchor 4 is what makes the zero-config case work. DSH installs profile plugins as
junction links and Node resolves them to their real path, so the plugin finds the
`config/models.json` shipped by the checkout it was installed from — no matter
where the host was launched. Anchor 3 covers the opposite case: a host started
inside a project that carries its own catalog.

readme.section: Where does the catalog come from?
readme.text:
> **Why the host's working directory and not the session's?** A plugin's `apply`
> runs when the profile boots — before any session exists — and one host serves
> many sessions with different workspaces, so there is no single "session working
> directory" to read at that moment. Anchors 1 and 2 are the explicit way to name
> a workspace. Per-session resolution is a deliberate future step, not an
> oversight; see [docs/roadmap.md](docs/roadmap.md).

readme.section: Where does the catalog come from?
readme.text:
If no anchor yields a catalog the plugin logs `model hub disabled` together with
**every directory it tried**, registers no tools, and lets DSH boot normally — a
missing or broken catalog never makes the agent unusable.

readme.section: Installing from a checkout instead of from GitHub
readme.text:
`dsh plugin add <path>` **links** the working tree — DSH installs profile plugins
as junction links — so Node resolves the plugin to its real path in the
repository instead of to a copy inside the profile. Peer dependencies then
resolve by walking up from the package: from `lib/dsh-plugin/` to
`<repo>/node_modules`. Run `npm install` once in the repository and that
directory exists, because `dsh plugin add` forwards to pnpm, which only *warns*
about peer dependencies instead of installing them.

readme.section: Installing from a checkout instead of from GitHub
readme.text:
This is not theoretical: it was found by installing into a throwaway profile,
deleting the workspace's `node_modules`, and watching the plugin fail to resolve
`@deepseek-ai/schemastery`.

A linked checkout also loads `lib/`, exactly like an installed copy does — so run
`npm run build` after editing `src/` or `dsh-plugin/`. If you would rather not
think about that, work on the hub as a library (`npm test`, `npm run typecheck`)
and only build when you want the plugin to pick the change up.

readme.section: Installing from a checkout instead of from GitHub
readme.text:
The historical obstacle on the GitHub route — Node refusing to strip types for
files under `node_modules` — is what committing `lib/` removes; see [Why the
package ships compiled JavaScript](#why-the-package-ships-compiled-javascript).

readme.section: What the agent can then do
readme.text:
| Ask the agent | Tool it calls |
|---|---|
| "What AI models can you run?" | `list_models` |
| "What can this machine actually do?" | `list_capabilities` |
| "Create a futuristic city image." | `invoke_model` (`text_to_image`) → router picks the model |
| "Now make a 3D model from that image." | `invoke_model` (`image_to_3d`), chaining the artifact id |
| "Why did it pick that model?" | `explain_routing` — read-only |
| "Is the image model running?" | `get_model_status`, `check_model_health` |
| "Start / stop the image model." | `start_model`, `stop_model` |

readme.section: What the agent can then do
readme.text: The agent never names an engine, a command, or a path. That is the whole design.

readme.section: The hub ships its own skill
readme.text:
The plugin also teaches the agent how to use it.
[`skills/dsh-ai-model-hub/SKILL.md`](skills/dsh-ai-model-hub/SKILL.md) is registered
as a skill provider on `ctx.skills`, the way DSH's own bundled `dsh-badge` skill is,
so:

readme.section: The hub ships its own skill
The hub ships its own skill
readme.text:
The registration is deliberately *not* a declared `inject`. It goes through
`ctx.inject(['skills'], …)`, so a composition with no skill registry — headless, or
the `sdk-minimal` profile — still gets the model tools and simply never runs the
skill callback. A missing or malformed skill file costs one warning and the skill,
never the tools beside it.

readme.section: The hub ships its own skill
readme.text:
The file is an ordinary skill, so it also works the old-fashioned way: link or copy
`skills/dsh-ai-model-hub/` into a `.dsh/skills` root if you would rather not run the
plugin at all. Its frontmatter is the single source of truth for the name and
description on both paths.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
The agent is not the only one who needs to know where the engines are. The plugin
also adds a **Local models** section to the DSH settings, which answers the question
a user actually has: which engines are on this PC, where is each one installed,
is it running, and what is inside it.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
| Row | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| Verified installation | Engine markers or executables in configured/well-known locations; a configured `cwd` alone is not proof |
| Configured paths | Catalog launch paths, displayed separately from verified installation paths |
| Listens on / availability | Independent bounded endpoint checks on both **Scan** and **Refresh** |
| Hub can start it | The descriptor's `startable`, after the deployment's `allowProcessLaunch` |
| Catalog models / capabilities | The same live hub the tools read, so the page cannot disagree with behaviour |

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
**Scan** is the page's main action, and it produces one list of two kinds of
thing, each row labelled with what it is:

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
| Kind | What it is | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **Ollama Model** | An observed or catalog-known model | Live `/api/tags`, offline loopback-host manifests (`OLLAMA_MODELS` or `~/.ollama/models`), active catalog, or last-good observations |
| **ComfyUI Workflow** | One complete workflow or an explained unreadable entry | Saved `/userdata` workflows, verified installation's workflow store, configured directories, and active catalog inline/pinned workflows |

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
A ComfyUI workflow is the smallest thing the list exposes. Its checkpoints,
LoRAs, VAEs, text encoders, ControlNets and individual nodes are **not** listed —
they are the workflow's own business, which is why changing what a workflow loads
never changes anything an agent or a user has to know.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
The two halves are discovered independently, so an Ollama instance that is down
cannot hide the workflows and a ComfyUI that is down cannot hide the models; each
source reports its own status. Scanning twice refreshes the list rather than
growing it, because every entry's id comes from its source location.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
**A saved workflow is discovered without a running ComfyUI.** Workflow discovery
reads the configured directories, the engine's own saved-workflow store when it
can be found on disk, the active catalog, and the workflows earlier scans
remembered — so a first launch with the engine stopped still lists the graphs that
are on the machine, and an engine that stops mid-session cannot take them off the
screen. The list says which evidence it has: `ComfyUI stopped` when a refused
connection proves the process is not running, `ComfyUI unreachable` when a timeout
or a routed address leaves that genuinely unknown, and a cached row whenever the
contract came from a previous observation rather than this pass. Only a scan that
completely read a source can conclude a workflow was deleted; a failure never can.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
The remembered workflows live in
`~/.dsh/plugins/dsh-ai-model-hub/workflow-catalog.json`, beside the capability
policy and for the same reason: it is machine state that changes without anyone
editing a file. It is per host *and* endpoint, so repointing the catalog at another
ComfyUI does not resurrect the old engine's workflows. `workflowCatalogPath`
configures it; `DSH_AI_MODEL_HUB_WORKFLOW_CATALOG` redirects it for a test.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
**Scan starts the configured engines; looking never does.** Opening or reloading the
page reads the machine as it finds it, and says what did not answer. Pressing
**Scan** is a deliberate act, so it checks each engine, starts any that is stopped
through the lifecycle manager's own launch path, polls its API until it answers
within a bounded budget, reads it, and finally releases its hold:

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Checking engines | Each engine's own readiness route is probed. An engine that answers is adopted and never restarted |
| Starting engines | A stopped engine is launched with the catalog's configured command; a missing command, a forbidden launch, or a refused spawn is reported with the setting that fixes it |
| Waiting for readiness | Bounded polling of the engine's API — a listening socket is not readiness. ComfyUI cold-starts get a longer default budget because loading checkpoints takes minutes |
| Scanning | Every readable engine is read: Ollama's models, ComfyUI's saved workflows |
| Complete / Partially complete | `complete` is false whenever an engine could not be started, timed out, died mid-read, or has no launch command, and the engine's own report says which and why |

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
While the scan reads, the engines it started are **held against automatic idle
unloading**; the hold is released in a `finally`, on success, failure and
cancellation alike, so a scan can never leave an engine permanently unsweepable. An
engine that was already running is neither started nor held — it is the user's
process, not the scan's. Repeated Scan clicks cannot start a second copy: the launch
goes through the same gate a cold invocation uses, which serializes transitions per
model, and a later scan simply reuses what is now running.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Engine states distinguish `running`, `installed_unreachable`, `not_found` in the
checked locations, and `unknown`. Connection failure alone proves neither that a
process is stopped nor that an installation is absent. The installation is the
directory whose *contents* are the engine — a ComfyUI whose `main.py` lives under
`src/` is installed at `src/`, which is also where its saved-workflow store hangs
from. Nothing is ever installed automatically.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Resource contract status is separate from availability. Each resource reports
`live`, `local`, `catalog`, or `cached` freshness and its observation timestamp.
An answering ComfyUI server does not verify a workflow's weights or execution;
local Ollama manifests do not verify every referenced blob. Failed refreshes keep
the last useful snapshot visibly stale; Retry requires no page reload. Superseded
requests cannot replace newer results or cache/provider publications.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ready` | Saved in API format — the hub queues it as it stands |
| `needs_conversion` | Saved in the editor's UI format. It is listed and converted for execution, but it is not the same as an API export |
| `invalid` | Readable, but produces nothing a caller can keep. The reason is shown |
| `unreadable` | The file or the engine's copy of it could not be retrieved. The transport reason is shown, because the document was never seen |
| `unavailable` | The engine needed to interpret it could not be reached |

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Running a remembered workflow while ComfyUI is stopped goes through the same
lifecycle manager as any other cold engine: the configured instance is started,
its readiness is awaited within the declared budget, and the graph is queued once it
answers. A startup that is refused or fails leaves the workflow listed with the
reason, and never falls through to a subscription provider — a workflow the user
picked is not silently swapped for a different one.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Runnable workflows are published to the hub as workflow-backed providers, so the
agent can route to them with the existing `invoke_model` tool by pinning the
workflow's id — the same harness, no second execution path. The public parameters
a workflow exposes (prompt, negative prompt, image, seed, steps, CFG, width,
height) are inferred from its graph and are the only fields a caller may set.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Engines the catalog does **not** declare are still listed — `a1111`, `comfyui`, and
`ollama` are known by name — with the directories that were checked, so "Forge is
installed but the hub has not been told" is visible instead of silent.

Two halves, both dependency-free:

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
- `dsh-plugin/inventory.ts` builds the answer and serves it on
  `GET /dsh-ai-model-hub/inventory`. Every probe is bounded and failures are
  contained; the route is injected on demand, so a headless profile with no web
  server keeps every tool and simply serves no page. The scan itself lives in
  `dsh-plugin/scan.ts`, and the graph → public-contract inference it uses is in
  `src/comfy/scan.ts`.
- `dsh-plugin/client.js` is the browser half. DSH loads plugin clients through
  `window.__ModuleLoader__` as plain side-effect scripts — no top-level
  `import`/`export`, React handed in through the factory's `require` — so this is
  hand-written JavaScript with **no bundler and no build step**, matching the rest
  of the project. It registers one `settings.section` contribution.

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
Configure a workflow directory when your workflows live beside the catalog rather
than inside ComfyUI:

```yaml
config:
  comfyuiWorkflowDir: 'C:/workflows/comfy'   # every *.json under it, recursively
  scanTimeoutMs: 4000                      # per-probe budget; filesystem walks are also capped
  workflowCatalogPath: ''                  # where discovered workflows are remembered

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
A relative directory is resolved against the catalog that configured it, and
`%VAR%` and `~/` are expanded from the host's own environment, so the same
configuration works on Windows and on a POSIX host. The directory is a source of
workflows only — nothing in it enumerates weights or custom nodes.

To see what a *stopped* engine still yields on this machine, with every HTTP probe
refusing:

readme.section: A settings page for what is on this machine
readme.text:
```bash
node scripts/verify-live-offline.ts                     # writes nothing
node scripts/verify-live-offline.ts ./scratch-catalog.json
```

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
Open **Settings → Local models**, then use the **Edit priorities** button at the
top left or the **Priorities** tab. The **Inventory** tab stays mounted alongside
the editor, so switching views or rescanning does not discard an unsaved draft.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
The editor uses responsive cards, human-readable capability names, provider
search, and **All / With options / Enabled** filters. Search matches capabilities
and their providers; it keeps each matching capability's full ordered list visible
so filtering never changes the meaning of a rank. Technical status and the policy
file are available in expandable details, and **Save / Cancel** stay reachable in
a sticky action bar. Light and dark colors follow the host theme.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
Each capability contains every option that genuinely declares it — local models,
ComfyUI workflows, and subscription backends in the *same* list, because to the hub
they are the same kind of thing: a way to serve a capability.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
On hosts that only report effective enablement while globally disabled, individual
editing is paused rather than guessing at saved permissions. Enable and save the
global switch to edit those options. Simply opening this page, switching tabs, or
changing filters never changes the policy or starts a model.

Three facts about an option are deliberately kept apart, and confusing them is the
failure this section exists to prevent:

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
| Fact | Where it lives | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| **Enabled / Disabled** | The policy you save | *May* this option serve this capability |
| **Position** | The policy you save | *When* it is tried, relative to the others |
| **State** | The live runtime | *Is* it usable right now — `ready`, `stopped`, `starting`, `unhealthy`, `unavailable`, `unsupported` |

So "disabled" is not "stopped", and "lower priority" is not "unavailable":

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
- A **disabled** option stays visible, marked `Disabled`, keeps its position, and is
  **never run** — not as a first choice and not as a fallback — and its engine is
  never started for it. Only you can change that.
- A **stopped but enabled and startable** local engine keeps its saved place and is
  started on demand. It is *not* demoted behind a remote backend that merely happens
  to be warm right now.
- A **lower-priority** option runs only after every higher-ranked permitted option
  has definitively failed.
- **Global disable wins over everything.** It is one switch, and it overrides every
  per-capability setting.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
Reordering is real drag-and-drop — and every row also has **Move up**, **Move down**,
**Move to top** and **Move to bottom** buttons with accessible names, so the list is
not mouse-only. Nothing is written until **Save**; **Cancel** reverts to the saved
policy. That matters for a list whose whole point is an arrangement: a drag that
saved immediately would make a mistake irreversible.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
The policy is persisted as its own versioned document, keyed by **stable ids**
(never display names), at `~/.dsh/plugins/dsh-ai-model-hub/capability-policy.json` —
override it with `policyPath`. It survives reloads, restarts, and catalog refreshes,
and an option that is temporarily undiscovered **keeps its saved settings** rather
than being forgotten.

readme.section: Capability priorities: order and enablement you own
readme.text:
**Nothing new activates itself.** A newly discovered option — a pulled Ollama model,
a workflow saved in ComfyUI, a subscription backend a plugin just registered —
appears in the list immediately, **disabled**, and stays that way until you enable
it. Catalog presence, a descriptor's own `enabled` flag, and visibility in a picker
are not authorization. Options that were already configured when the plugin loaded
keep working exactly as they did, so the feature is a no-op on an existing
deployment until you touch it.

readme.section: How a request is served
readme.text:
1. Inputs are resolved and validated against the artifact store.
2. Global enablement, then the capability's own enablement, are applied.
3. Your saved order decides the sequence.
4. Compatibility and live readiness are checked — **without demoting a startable
   stopped engine**.
5. A permitted local engine is made ready: a warm one is reused, a startup already in
   progress is joined rather than duplicated, and a cold one is started with its
   configured command. The **readiness check** gates the submission — process
   creation or an open port alone is not enough.
6. The request is dispatched to that **exact** backend and no other.
7. On an eligible definitive failure, the next permitted compatible option is tried.
8. When the permitted list is exhausted, the hub stops and reports every reason.

readme.section: How a request is served
readme.text:
There is **no attempt cap by default**: a saved order of ten options really is ten
attempts. A deployment that needs a smaller budget sets `attemptBudget`, and the
failure message then says how many options went untried rather than implying they
failed.

readme.section: Readiness, not liveness
readme.text:
A bare `2xx` proves that *something* is listening. It does not prove the engine can
serve work — a half-loaded engine or any local web page answers `200` too, and this
project has been bitten by exactly that. A health check may therefore demand the
shape of a real answer:

```json
"health": {
  "kind": "http",
  "path": "/system_stats",
  "expect": "json-key",

readme.section: Readiness, not liveness
readme.text:
`any` (the default) keeps the historical permissive behaviour; `json` requires a JSON
body; `json-key` additionally requires one of `expectKeys` at the top level. A body
that fails the expectation is an **unhealthy** model with the observed content in the
reason. The shipped catalog uses this for ComfyUI (`/system_stats`) and Ollama
(`/api/tags`).

readme.section: Turning automatic startup on or off
readme.text:
Automatic local-engine startup is the deployment-level `allowProcessLaunch` switch,
and it has always been the one place to decide it — once, not per request:

```yaml
config:
  allowProcessLaunch: true    # the hub may start an engine its catalog declares startable
```

readme.section: Turning automatic startup on or off
readme.text:
Both halves must agree: the descriptor declares `lifecycle.startable: true` with a
`start` command, *and* the deployment opts in. With launching off, an engine that is
merely stopped is reported as **not startable by the hub** with that as the reason —
never launched anyway, and never confused with a failed launch. See
[`docs/security.md`](docs/security.md) before enabling it.

readme.section: Seeing what happened
readme.text:
`invoke_model` reports the requested capability, the **policy revision** that decided
it, the ordered list of permitted options, everything that was skipped with the
switch or fact that skipped it, and how each attempt turned out — distinguishing
**launch forbidden**, **stopped**, **startup failed**, and **generation failed** by
the stage it failed at. That is reported on success too: "why did this run on the
second option?" is answered by the first option's reason, not by a log hunt.

readme.section: If the outcome cannot be determined
readme.text:
A timeout or a dropped connection **after** the request reached the backend leaves a
question this process cannot answer: did it generate? The hub refuses to guess. It
reports an explicit **unresolved** outcome, with any identifiers that can be used to
look the work up, and does **not** fall back — because generating again could
double-charge a subscription or repeat a three-minute render. A refusal the backend
*stated* (quota, a login problem, a `4xx`) is a definitive "no", and the plan moves
on as usual.

readme.section: Pointing the hub at your engines
readme.text:
The shipped catalog ([`config/models.json`](config/models.json)) declares two real
engines — Ollama for text and ComfyUI for images — and includes a specific ComfyUI
workflow provider. Ensure Ollama has the configured model and ComfyUI has the
workflow's required weights; installing a new checkpoint or saving a workflow does
not, on its own, register a new ComfyUI provider.

readme.section: Pointing the hub at your engines
readme.text:
To change them, or to add more, edit that file or point the plugin at your own
with `configPath` / `searchRoots`. Everything else is copy-and-adjust from
[`config/examples/real-models.example.json`](config/examples/real-models.example.json):
an A1111/Forge/sd.cpp server uses `http_json`, llama.cpp uses
`openai_compatible`, and ComfyUI uses its own `comfyui` adapter driven by a graph
template — an example is in
[`config/workflows/z-image-turbo.api.json`](config/workflows/z-image-turbo.api.json),
an API-format `{client_id, prompt}` graph. The provider additionally declares exact
`bindings` for caller inputs and an `outputs` node/type selector; the graph's
internals are not inferred. To add a ComfyUI provider, configure the host's
`adapterConfig.workflows` with `id`, `name`, `workflowPath`, `capabilities`,
`bindings`, `outputs` and optional routing/resource settings. The static model
alternative uses `adapterConfig.providerKind: "workflow"` and `workflowId`.

readme.section: Pointing the hub at your engines
readme.text:
A catalog names those files (`workflowPath` for ComfyUI, `stepsPath` for 3D) with
paths **relative to the catalog itself**, because a catalog can live anywhere and
the process that reads it can be started from anywhere. The shipped
[`config/models.json`](config/models.json) therefore says
`workflows/z-image-turbo.api.json` — `config/` is that file's own directory —
while the same template from inside `config/examples/` is
`../workflows/z-image-turbo.api.json`. Absolute paths also work. A path that does
not resolve names itself and its base in the error rather than guessing.

readme.section: Pointing the hub at your engines
readme.text:
A wrong model name is a loud failure — the engine answers 404 and the invocation
fails — never fixture text: there are no mock models in any shipped catalog. See
[docs/adding-a-model.md](docs/adding-a-model.md).

readme.section: Let the engines list their own models
readme.text:
For supported enumerating engines such as Ollama, set `discoverModels: true` on
the plugin to register pulled models. **ComfyUI remains workflow-only and
configuration-driven**: discovery does not publish its loose checkpoints or saved
workflows. Add a ComfyUI workflow descriptor to the host config (or a static
workflow model) and reload the catalog:

```yaml
- insert:
    - id: dsh-ai-model-hub
      name: 'dsh-ai-model-hub'
      config:

readme.section: Let the engines list their own models
readme.text:
It is **off by default**, and off means no engine is ever contacted for
introspection. With it on:

readme.section: Let the engines list their own models
readme.text:
- `config/models.json` still wins. A discovered model whose id a hand-written
  entry claims is dropped before the catalog is built, so the file stays the
  place to set exact resources or fix priority. ComfyUI workflow providers are
  always explicitly configured, independently of this discovery switch.
- An engine that is down is a warning in the log, never a failed boot.
- Results are cached per host for `discoveryTtlMs` (60 s). The
  `refresh_model_discovery` tool bypasses the cache — that is the path right
  after `ollama pull`.
- Resource figures for discovered models are estimates (from a reported file
  size where the engine gives one, from the filename otherwise), good enough to
  keep an oversized model off a small card and not a specification.

readme.section: Let the engines list their own models
readme.text:
Discovery never bypasses `resolveDescriptor()`: it produces descriptors in the
same shape as a `models.json` entry, and the router, runtime manager, and
adapters are unchanged by it. See
[docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md#4-host--model--runtime-discovery).

Nothing is launched by default: `allowProcessLaunch` is `false`, so the hub talks
to engines you run but will not start any. See
[docs/security.md](docs/security.md) before turning that on.

readme.section: Where the output goes
readme.text:
Artifacts land in **`<workspace>/artifacts`**, where "workspace" means the
*calling session's*, not the host process's working directory. That distinction is
the whole point: `dsh web` is one long-lived process serving many sessions with
different workspaces, and it is built — and used to resolve this path — before any
session exists. So the root is resolved per tool call, from DSH's own
`ctx.sandboxPolicy.resolve({ session }).workspaceRoot`, which is the same value the
file tools treat as the workspace boundary.

readme.section: Where the output goes
readme.text:
The consequence a user notices: switch workspace in the GUI and output follows,
with no configuration. `list_artifacts` reads the same per-call root, so chaining a
workflow still finds what the previous step produced.

readme.section: Where the output goes
readme.text:
Set `artifactRoot` in the plugin row to pin one absolute directory for every
session instead — the right choice when collecting artifacts centrally, the wrong
one when you want each conversation's images beside its code. The hub refuses a
relative root rather than guessing at a base.

readme.section: Where the output goes
readme.text:
Turn it on and engines start themselves. A descriptor that marks its engine
startable — `"startable": true` plus a `start` command, as the `a1111` host in
[`config/examples/real-models.example.json`](config/examples/real-models.example.json)
does — lets `start_model` bring the engine up, and lets `invoke_model` do it
implicitly for a cold model, waiting for the health check before the request is
sent. A stopped ComfyUI then costs one cold start, not a failed task:

readme.section: Where the output goes
readme.text:
```
invoke_model({ capability: 'text_to_image', prompt: 'a red fox in deep snow' })
  → text_to_image served by comfyui_z_image_turbo in 22620 ms (cold start).
```

Two switches have to agree — the descriptor's `startable` and the deployment's
`allowProcessLaunch` — so an 8 GB model cannot be started by a catalog file alone.
Starting an engine that is already healthy is a no-op rather than a duplicate
process, and only processes the hub started can be stopped by `stop_model`.

readme.section: The five-minute mental model
The five-minute mental model
readme.text:
**A model is data, not code.** Adding one means adding a JSON entry:

```json
{
  "id": "a1111_sdxl",
  "name": "SDXL (WebUI)",
  "type": "image_generation",

No router change. No prompt change. No DSH change.

**Artifacts are the only thing that crosses a model boundary.** That is what
makes `text → image → 3D` compose without anything knowing about PNG or GLB:

readme.section: The five-minute mental model
What is where
readme.text:
```
dsh-ai-model-hub/
├── src/                          the hub — imports NOTHING from DeepSeek Harness
│   ├── catalog/                  capability vocabulary, descriptor schema, registry,
│   │                             published JSON Schema

readme.section: What is where
readme.text:
**The dependency rule that makes this survivable:** `src/` does not import
`@deepseek-ai/*`. Only `dsh-plugin/` does. DSH is a `0.1.x-rc` line, so breaking
changes are expected; when one lands, the blast radius is the plugin layer, and
the entire hub keeps working and keeps passing its tests.

readme.section: Try it without any engine
readme.text:
```sh
npm test          # the whole suite; real HTTP servers stand in for engines
npm run demo:3d   # discovery → routing → a real .glb → the boundary transcript
npm run demo      # capability discovery and routing against your own catalog
```

readme.section: Requirements
readme.text:
- **Node ≥ 22.6** — the hub *sources* run directly through Node's type stripping
  while you work in a checkout. The installed package loads the compiled `lib/`
  instead, because Node refuses to strip types under `node_modules`;
  `npm run build` regenerates it.
- **pnpm** — only for `dsh plugin`, which forwards to it.
- **No runtime dependencies.** The hub is dependency-free by design: a plugin
  whose `node_modules` must resolve inside a DSH profile is a plugin that breaks
  on the next release. The DSH packages it imports are peers, supplied by the
  profile that loads it.
